Site-owned and standard-only: there is no user layer, deliberately -- a private workspace is already yours to edit directly, and a public one is the site's. The merge is split on purpose. Roles, icon, visibility and sequence are a true diff, so an app's later changes to them keep flowing through. Content is a snapshot, so customizing the layout freezes it against app updates: workspace content is nested editor blocks where headings, paragraphs and spacers carry no key at all, and a delta cannot be written against unkeyed prose. One entry on the dock. `link_type` says what kind of thing it opens, and each kind answers the two questions a click asks -- which page comes up and which shell comes up beside it -- in its own way. A `Sidebar` row *is* the shell: it selects that sidebar and opens its landing route. A `Workspace` row opens a page and derives its shell from the module that owns it. A `URL` row leaves the desk and has no shell at all. Every row also carries its own `icon` and `title`, so the rail reads the way its author wrote it -- blank at an upper layer means inherit. What a row points at *is* its identity, and none of it is stored: re-labelling cannot detach a row from itself, and re-pointing is not an edit but a different row. The same rows at all three layers -- the app's own dock, the site's arrangement and one person's -- told apart by the parent `Dock`, never by the row.

One layer of one app's dock. Three of them share this table, told apart by `app`, `user` and `standard`: the app's own dock, which an app ships as an exported document and a developer authors; the site's arrangement of it, curated by a Workspace Manager and applying to everyone; and one person's own, applied last and winning. A dock belongs to an app, so arranging ERPNext's rail does not touch frappe's -- and a layer is addressed by app plus user rather than by user alone. Same shape at all three, because the rows are identical and the parent is what says whose they are; see `Custom Sidebar`, which layers a sidebar the same way in a table of its own.

One ordered list holding both references to base items (`added` unset -- non-empty fields override, empty fields mean no opinion) and items this layer added (`added` set -- full items, rendered as they stand). Row order is the arrangement; base items not named here keep their base order and follow the ones that are, which is how a newly installed app's items still reach someone who has already reordered.

Spelled the way `Sidebar Item` spells it, so `frappe.ui.sidebar_item.get_route(row)` takes the two page kinds unchanged. `Sidebar` is a value here because a module entry is an entry like any other: it opens the shell, which is the one destination that is not a page.

What the rail draws this entry with. Required when the row *adds* an entry, because nothing below it holds one; optional when it references an entry a lower layer already has, where blank means inherit and filled is an override.

What this sidebar is called, on screen and as its record name (`autoname: field:title`). Defaults to the module's name, and the default is stored -- so a module's own sidebar keeps the name it has always had, and a second sidebar under that module is told apart by being called something else. `unique` on top of that adds one thing the primary key does not: it refuses a second sidebar claiming the title of a row whose name has drifted away from it -- a legacy row, or one written straight to the table.
